items.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: No, first I had Jimmy Heath and Cedar Walton and Sam Jones and Mickey Roker.

ctx.x: What was your opinion or impression when all of a sudden John Coltrane starts to expand his…

When I first met Trane, he came out to Los Angeles with a group that Dizzy had put together. It was Trane and Jimmy Heath on the saxophone, Percy Heath was playing bass, Specs Wright from Philadelphia was playing drums, and Milt Jackson was in the group. They didn’t have a pianist, so everybody took turns playing the piano. I met Trane then, and that’s the first time I heard him play. He sounded fine, but to me, he was just another young guy like everybody else trying to get it together. By the time he organized…
Even before McCoy Tyner joined the group, John Coltrane had recorded Giant Steps. Did that have an impact on you? Do you recall hearing that for the first time?

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Art Farmer, and others, that I’ve come into contact with, and performed with

ctx.x: And how did you structure it?

Well, it is a compilation of all the giants who are still here, and some who are gone, their words endorsing me in a lot of cases, or speaking of experiences we had together. In doing so, I was very fortunate to have a few words from John Coltrane, from Dizzy. Those who are past on [such as] Art Farmer, and others, that I’ve come into contact with, and performed with, and had good times or bad times with.
Well, it’s a lot of time to cover so I imagine, you know, [it was] no small task. Is it something you’ve worked on sporadically over the years or have you been diligently putting it together?
